title: Samson Occom
summary: Samson Occom, also written Sampson Occum or Samson Occam, was a Mohegan minister, teacher, writer, and Native political leader whose life connected Mohegan, Montaukett, Shinnecock, Oneida, and Brothertown histories.
content:
Samson Occom (1723–July 14, 1792), also written Sampson Occum or Samson Occam, was a Mohegan minister, teacher, writer, and Native political leader whose life connected Mohegan, Montaukett, Shinnecock, Oneida, and Brothertown histories.

He became one of the most widely known Native Christian writers and public figures of the eighteenth century, while also working for Native education and intertribal community-building.12

Historical Context

On December 6, 1743, Occom went to study with Rev. Eleazar Wheelock at Lebanon, Connecticut.1

From 1749 to 1761, he taught and ministered at Montauk, where he married Mary Fowler and became deeply connected with Montaukett community life.13

Occom was examined and ordained by the Presbytery of Long Island in East Hampton on August 29-30, 1759.1

From 1765 to 1768, he traveled to Great Britain to raise funds for Moor's Indian Charity School, preaching to large audiences.1

Later, Occom became a leading architect of the Brothertown movement, helping Native families from Long Island and New England build an intertribal community in what is now upstate New York.1

Quoted Voice

In his 1768 autobiographical narrative, Occom began by locating himself at Mohegan: I was born a Heathen and Brought up in Heathenism, till I was between 16 & 17 Years of age, at a Place Calld Mohegan...1

References

  1. Joanna Brooks, ed., The Collected Writings of Samson Occom, Mohegan, pp. 349-350, 368, 421.
  2. William DeLoss Love, Samson Occom and the Christian Indians of New England.
  3. Gaynell Stone, The History and Archaeology of the Montauk.
why_this_matters: Occom shows Indigenous intellectual leadership and community-building across regional boundaries. His story connects Long Island Native history with education, religion, writing, migration, and Native-led survivance.
